name: Gareth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a farm worker at Greystone, a big estate, about fifteen hundred hectares of wheat and oilseed rape plus three hundred suckler cows, the ones that rear their own calves. I start at seven, feed and check the cattle with Marcus, the stockman, then usually I'm on a tractor or sorting out the GPS on the sprayer. I did IT support for the council for fifteen years before this. Eighteen months in, I can fix any screen on the estate but I'm still learning which end of a cow kicks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being outside, I lost three stone in my first year. And I like being useful, the manager, Helen, pays me above the usual farm rate because I set up the drone mapping and fix the auto-steer. The hard bit is the stock work. Marcus can spot a lame cow from across a field, I need to see it limp three times.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lucia's a pharmacist at the county hospital, she checks prescriptions and advises the doctors. Mateo's eleven and Ana's eight. We sold our house in the city and bought a smaller one out here, so there's a good chunk left in savings, well over a year. I use AI every day, asking it about cattle diseases, planning my week, even writing Helen's spray records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: it's a useful tool and people overhyped it, both the doomsayers and the salesmen. I'd probably post a long thing about how the real gains were always in boring places like spray records. Most people in the farm canteen wouldn't care either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. I left a desk job to get away from screens, and I still end up being the guy who fixes the estate's GPS. That's why I'm paid well. If nothing radical changes, I keep doing what I do, and I keep getting better at the cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for records and planning and ask Helen to let me do the cattle handling course in January. I'd keep the savings in the bank and carry on as normal. Maybe I'd teach Marcus to use the herd app, though he'd resist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. A bit let down, if anything, because I find this stuff exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show Marcus first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bit where you take a photo of a cow's feet and it suggests what's wrong. Marcus would say he already knows what's wrong, and he'd be right, but it'd help me when he's off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Lucia's work change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Some of the routine checks would get faster. Lucia would grumble about a new system for six months and then forget it was ever different.

say: AI is a **useful tool** that both doomsayers and salesmen overhyped.
The real gains were always in **boring places** like spray records.
think: He's paid well because he **fixes the GPS**, which this world doesn't change.
He can keep **learning the cattle** at his own pace.
do: **Keep** using AI for spray records and weekly planning.
**Ask** Helen for the cattle handling course in January.
**Teach** Marcus the herd app's foot photo feature.
feel: **Content**, if a little let down because he finds AI exciting.
S0.quote: I left a desk job to get away from screens, and I still end up being the guy who fixes the estate's GPS.
fieldNote: An **ex-IT worker** whose tech skill is what earns him above-rate farm pay.
**Strong savings** from selling a city house; no money pressure at all.
Mild disappointment that **nothing happens**, unusual among farm workers.

steps.text: Do the cattle handling course at Greystone in January
Show Marcus the herd app's foot photo feature

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the estate should use it, but the workers should have a say in how. I'd push for a proper agreement at Greystone: if AI saves money, some goes into wages and training. I'd be the one in the canteen explaining what the thinking tasks actually are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good, I'm the one who'd set it up. The worry is Lucia. My wife checks prescriptions for a living, and that's exactly the kind of checking this card says goes first. The hospital wouldn't sack her, but they'd stop replacing pharmacists when they leave, and her workload would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put a plan to Helen for drone spot-spraying and AI field planning, with me running it. I'd join the farm workers' union and ask them to push for a technology agreement at Greystone. And I'd sit down with Lucia and look at the patient-facing side of her job, the clinics, which are harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for me, uneasy for Lucia. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Lucia say when you raised it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia laughed and said the software can't argue with a consultant at two in the morning. Then she went quiet and said she'd look at the clinic course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd bring in the drones yourself. Doesn't that cut somebody's hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might cut some spraying hours, yes, maybe Dave's. That's why I'd want the agreement first, so Dave moves into something, not out the door. I'm not naive about it.

say: Greystone should use AI, but **workers need a say** in how it's brought in.
If AI saves money, some should go into **wages and training**.
think: His own role **grows**, because he'd be the one setting up the tools.
His wife's **prescription checking** is exactly the thinking work that goes first.
do: **Propose** drone spot-spraying and AI field planning to Helen, run by him.
**Join** the farm workers' union and push for a technology agreement.
**Plan** with Lucia a move towards patient clinics.
feel: **Excited** for himself and **uneasy** for Lucia, both at once.
S1.quote: My wife checks prescriptions for a living, and that's exactly the kind of checking this card says goes first.
fieldNote: Household exposure sits with his **partner**, not with him.
He'd **automate** his own farm but insists on a worker agreement first.
Openly admits the drones might cut **Dave's hours**, a candid moment.

steps.text: Propose drone spot-spraying at Greystone with himself running it
Join the farm workers' union and ask for a technology agreement
Help Lucia apply for the hospital's patient clinic course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest change in history and we're letting a few companies decide it. Public ownership, a dividend for everyone, proper retraining, I'd be posting about it every day. And I'd tell the lads at work not to waste time being angry at the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My thinking work is small, so 2028 hits Lucia more than me. Her hospital checking role could be mostly gone by then. Then 2031 is when the robots come for the tractor seat and the cattle yard. I'd happily be the person who keeps the robots running, as long as the people they replace get a share of what they earn. But I'm honest that robots that good might not need much minding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd sign up for the agricultural robotics certificate at the college, the one-year evening course. Lucia would move into clinics before the hospital decides for her. We'd hold off on the house extension and keep the savings ready. And I'd join any campaign for a citizens' dividend, money paid to everyone from the profits of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. Lucia's job and mine both in five years is a lot, even with savings. But I'd feel I had a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extension, definitely, we were going to build a playroom for Ana. And the second car, I'd sell it and cycle to Greystone in summer. It's four miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo to learn to build things and to talk to people, and to never let anyone tell him a machine is magic. Then I'd show him how the drone works, because he'd ask.

say: We're letting **a few companies** decide the biggest change in history.
We need **public ownership** and a dividend for everyone from AI profits.
think: 2028 hits **Lucia's job** harder than his, as hospital checking work disappears.
By 2031 robots may need **little minding**, which threatens even his tech role.
do: **Enrol** in the one-year agricultural robotics evening certificate.
**Shelve** the playroom extension and sell the second car.
**Campaign** for a citizens' dividend from AI profits.
feel: **Properly worried**, with two jobs at risk within five years.
Still feels he has **a hand** on the wheel.
S2.quote: I'd happily be the person who keeps the robots running, as long as the people they replace get a share of what they earn.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** protects him but not his wife's thinking work.
Self-aware that robot-minding jobs may be **few**, tempering his optimism.
Moves fast: **course, cuts and campaign** all start in the first year.

steps.text: Enrol in the one-year agricultural robotics evening certificate
Sell the second car and shelve the playroom extension
Campaign for a citizens' dividend paid from AI profits
Help Lucia move into hospital clinic work before 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if we start policy now: training paid for, a dividend, workers on company boards. I'd say the same stuff, just a bit less shouty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to stop being a junior farmhand and become the estate's robot mechanic. Lucia has time to settle into clinics. By 2034, when the robots are good enough, I'd have three years of running them. I think we come out fine, but the people around us won't all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics certificate over two years instead of one, and get Helen to trial the first field robots with me around 2032. I'd keep the extension on hold until we see 2031. I'd push the union for an agreement that whoever is displaced at Greystone gets training money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit watchful. I'd be thinking about Marcus and Dave more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Marcus and Dave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus is fifty-nine and won't touch a screen. Dave's my age but hates school, he said a classroom makes his skin crawl. They're the ones who need the deal, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings for anything here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe put some into the course and a decent laptop, nothing big. I'd rather keep the cushion until I see what 2031 looks like.

say: **Five years** is short but workable if policy starts now.
Put **workers on boards** and pay for training and a dividend.
think: He could move from junior farmhand to the estate's **robot mechanic** by 2034.
His family likely **comes out fine**; the people around them might not.
do: **Complete** the robotics certificate over two years.
**Trial** the first field robots with Helen around 2032.
**Push** the union for training money for displaced Greystone staff.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a bit watchful, thinking of Marcus and Dave.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to stop being a junior farmhand and become the estate's robot mechanic.
fieldNote: More time lets him **slow down** the same plan.
His concern shifts to **older colleagues** who won't retrain.
Keeps the **cushion** intact until he sees 2031.

steps.text: Complete the robotics certificate part-time over two years
Trial the first field robots at Greystone with Helen around 2032
Push the union for training money for displaced Greystone staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if we're serious, and nobody gets to say they weren't warned. I'd talk about who owns the machines, because that decides who gets richer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine for me. By 2039 I'm fifty-six, robot mechanic or estate manager, and the kids are through university. I'd rather the robots belonged to a farmers' co-op than to the company that sold the estate its tractors. That's the part I'd fight about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning, keep using AI every day, do the robotics course in my own time. I'd put some savings into a local machinery co-op, where farms share the cost of robots. And I'd keep pushing Helen to share the gains with staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely looking forward to parts of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a machinery co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farms club together to buy expensive kit and share it, so a small farm doesn't have to buy a whole robot. Ours already shares a big combine harvester. Robots would be the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that bothers you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone will relax because ten years sounds long. Councils plan in five-year chunks, they'd miss it.

say: A decade is **plenty** if we're serious; nobody can say they weren't warned.
**Who owns** the machines decides who gets richer.
think: By 2039 he expects to be a **robot mechanic** or estate manager.
He'd want robots owned by a **farmers' co-op**, not a dealer company.
do: **Take** the robotics course in his own time.
**Invest** savings in the local machinery co-op's robot fund.
**Press** Helen to share gains with staff.
feel: **Calm** and genuinely looking forward to parts of it.

fieldNote: Ten years removes the **household risk** and leaves only politics.
Puts money where his views are: a **machinery co-op** share.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lucia's work goes first and then mine three years on. What would help is free retraining that pays you while you learn, and a dividend from AI profits so nobody's left with nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the irony. I moved to the country to escape computers, and it turns out I'm the one bringing them in. I don't mind, but I'd like it to be on fair terms.

headlineQuote: I moved to the country to escape computers, and it turns out I'm the one bringing them in.
portrait: Former **council IT** worker, eighteen months into farming on a large arable and beef estate.
Paid **above farm rate** because he runs the drones, GPS and auto-steer.
Daily AI user whose household risk sits with his **pharmacist wife**.
Calm in the plateau, **anxious** at AGI by 2028 when both jobs shift within five years.
Wants robots **co-owned** and gains shared, and would retrain as a robot mechanic.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as Lucia's checking work goes first and his job three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A **dividend** from AI profits for everyone.
